adopted.summary: New npm/ package @seerly/mcp: own stdio-to-Streamable-HTTP bridge on @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, browser OAuth via a loopback callback, credentials in ~/.seerly/mcp; tag-triggered GitHub Actions publish with provenance.
adopted.rationale:
- Repo holds no server code; the package can only relay to https://seerly.app/api/mcp
- Backend already advertises registration, S256 PKCE, token auth none: no backend change
- SDK does registration, PKCE and refresh; provider only stores and opens the browser
- Credentials re-read from disk on every use: backend rotates refresh tokens
- Callback listener lives for the process: redirect URL needed before any 401
- Tag-version check stops a mismatched release
- Exact pins match the repo root (SDK 1.32.2, TypeScript, @types/node)

tour.title: Stdio bridge to the remote server
tour.what:
- Relays each stdio message to Seerly over Streamable HTTP, and each reply back (`Bridge`)
- Waits on one shared browser sign-in after an `UnauthorizedError`, then resends (`signIn`, `signingIn`)
- Answers any other failed request with a JSON-RPC InternalError (`answerWithError`)
- Sets the protocol version agreed in `initialize` on the remote transport (`deliver`)
- Wires URL, callback server, store, provider and bridge; exits when stdin ends (`cli.ts`)
tour.why:
- Repo is plugin-only; the server lives in airo-backend at /api/mcp
- Own bridge on the official SDK rather than mcp-remote (see trials)
- Later requests must carry the negotiated protocol version
tour.attention: A request whose sign-in is abandoned is never answered; no timeout

tour.title: Pinned-project mode and server URL
tour.what:
- Appends a URL-encoded project argument, pinning every tool to it (`resolveServerUrl`)
- Takes the base from `SEERLY_MCP_URL`, else https://seerly.app/api/mcp; strips trailing slashes
tour.why:
- Mirrors the remote `https://seerly.app/api/mcp/<domain>` form
- Staging slots reachable without a rebuild
tour.attention: Pinned URL gets its own credential file, client and sign-in

tour.title: Browser sign-in and local credentials
tour.what:
- Listens on 127.0.0.1, random port, `/callback`, for the bridge's lifetime (`CallbackServer`)
- Accepts only the latest sign-in's `state`; hands its code to whoever waits
- Registers as a public client (no secret) with that loopback redirect (`SeerlyOAuthProvider`)
- Keeps the PKCE verifier in memory; persists client and tokens
- Refuses authorization URLs outside the server's origin
- Stores client and tokens in one 0600 file per server URL under `~/.seerly/mcp`, re-read on every use (`CredentialStore`)
- Writes via temp file plus rename
- Opens the browser via `open` / `rundll32` / `xdg-open`, no shell (`openBrowser`)
tour.why:
- Backend rotates refresh tokens and revokes the family on reuse
- Re-reading lets a second bridge see the newest pair
- Backend accepts loopback redirects on any port: one stored client survives a new port per process
- Redirect URL must exist before the first 401
tour.attention: Concurrent 401s each start a new authorization: new state, new verifier, another tab

tour.title: Package manifest, lockfile and build
tour.what:
- Declares `@seerly/mcp` 0.1.0 with bin `seerly-mcp` -> `dist/cli.js`; ships only `dist`
- Publishes public with provenance; `repository.url` points at Seerly-AI/seerly-mcp, directory npm
- Pins SDK, TypeScript, @types/node and engines to the repo root's values
- Locks the tree `npm ci` builds in CI (`package-lock.json`)
- Compiles strict ES2022/NodeNext from src to dist (`tsconfig.json`)
tour.why:
- Trusted publishing matches `repository.url` exactly
- Root package.json stays private
- `npm ci` fails without the lockfile
tour.attention: `engines >=20.11` inherited from root; npm/ code needs only >=20

tour.title: Tag-triggered publish workflow and release procedure
tour.what:
- Publishes `npm/` when any `npm-v*` tag is pushed
- Fails unless the tag equals `npm-v` plus the package.json version
- Installs npm 11.21.1; grants `id-token: write` for OIDC and provenance
- Copies the root LICENSE into the package before publishing
- Passes `NPM_TOKEN` as `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN`, meant for the first release only
- Documents the release: bump version, merge, tag from main (root README)
tour.why:
- npm cannot trust a workflow for a package that does not exist yet
- Publishing from CI keeps the deploy-only-from-git rule
- Tarball carries no licence without the copy
tour.attention: Nothing restricts the tag to main; token line stays until a follow-up commit

tour.title: Setup docs
tour.what:
- Points stdio-only apps to `npx -y @seerly/mcp` (root README)
- Lists `npm/` in the repo layout
- Gives the config snippet for Claude Desktop, Cursor and Windsurf (`npm/README.md`)
- Documents the single-project argument, credentials folder and Node floor
tour.why:
- npm/README ships in the tarball and shows on npmjs.com
- No revoke-access line: the app has no revoke UI
tour.attention: Snippets untried in any real app; 'readable only by you' checked on macOS only

evaluated.question: npm/package.json sets `engines.node` to `>=20.11` and the README repeats it. The SDK says >=18 and @hono/node-server >=20. Where does 20.11 specifically come from?
evaluated.answer:
Inference, but grounded in what the session read: it was inherited from the repo root.
- At entry 42 the session ran `cat package.json`. The root seerly-mcp package.json declares `"engines": { "node": ">=20.11" }`.
- It also pins the same versions npm/package.json uses: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.2, `@types/node` 22.10.2, `typescript` 5.6.3.
- The session also read `scripts/generate-references.ts`, at the step it described as "read existing script conventions".
- npm/package.json mirrors the root on all four.

In the root, 20.11 is justified: `scripts/generate-references.ts` uses `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename`, which arrived in Node 20.11.

In npm/ it is not specifically needed:
- A grep of npm/src finds no `import.meta` use.
- The code needs only ES2022 and `??=`.
- The floor actually binding is the dependencies: SDK `>=18`, its `@hono/node-server` `>=20`.
- So `>=20` would be the real minimum. 20.11 is a carried-over convention.

The session never stated a reason, and only Node 22.22.0 was exercised.

unresolved.question: Sign-in has no timeout: if the user closes or ignores the browser tab, `signIn()` / `nextCode()` never settle, so the request that hit the 401 is never answered (the Bridge doc says "the app never waits on it"). Separately, desktop MCP clients time out `initialize` on their own (the TS SDK client default is 60 s). Did the session consider either: what the app does if initialize times out while the user is still on the consent page, and whether the bridge should give up on a sign-in after N minutes?
unresolved.note:
The transcript does not settle this. Neither a bridge-side sign-in timeout nor desktop clients' own initialize timeouts was discussed. I grepped the session for timeout and initialize discussion; nothing turned up beyond what is listed here.

What the session did see:
- `initialize` blocks for the whole sign-in. The e2e test client had to raise its own connect timeout to accommodate it, from 600_000 ms to 1_800_000 ms.
- Run 1 failed with "McpError: MCP error -32001: Request timed out ... { timeout: 600000 }". That was the test client's timeout while nobody consented. It was not a bridge timeout.
- The assistant's response was a longer test window ("this time with a 30-minute window to sign in"), not a change to the bridge.
- The passing run initialized after 16 s, well inside any client default.

Inference from code:
- `CallbackServer.nextCode()` returns a promise that only settles when the callback is hit. There is no timer.
- `Bridge.signIn()` waits on it indefinitely, so an ignored or closed tab leaves that request unanswered for the life of the process.
- The "the app never waits on it" doc line in bridge.ts only covers requests that fail.
- If the app times out initialize first, the bridge keeps listening. A sign-in completed later still saves tokens to `~/.seerly/mcp/`, so the next app start works without a prompt. That late recovery was not tested.
- Whether clients such as Claude Desktop, Cursor or Windsurf time out initialize, and after how long, was never checked.

Open intent question for the developer: whether to add a give-up timeout. Not decided in the session.

unresolved.question: Two requests that both get a 401 in the same process each run a fresh SDK `auth()`: each calls `state()` (overwriting the expected state), `saveCodeVerifier()` (overwriting the verifier) and `redirectToAuthorization()` (opening a second browser tab). Only the latest tab can complete; earlier tabs show "expired"; and if the later auth lands after the first code arrives but before `finishAuth` reads the verifier, the token exchange fails PKCE. `signingIn` dedupes the wait but not the authorization start. Was this considered, and was deduping at `redirectToAuthorization`/`state()` discussed?
unresolved.note:
Not discussed in the conversation. The only trace of the design is in the code the session wrote:
- bridge.ts: "One browser sign-in at a time: messages turned away meanwhile wait for the same one."
- callback-server.ts: `expect()` uses `this.pending ??=`, with the comment "its code goes to whoever already waits". It also accepts "only the state of the latest sign-in".
I grepped the session for the double-tab or PKCE race; nothing. Visible thinking is encrypted, so I cannot say whether it was weighed privately.

Inference, from reading SDK 1.32.2 `client/streamableHttp.js` `send()` (lines 328-348) and `auth.js`:
- On a 401, each `send()` calls `auth()` itself. With no refresh token, that calls `provider.state()`, then `saveCodeVerifier()`, then `redirectToAuthorization()`.
- So the reviewer's reading is right: two concurrent 401s open two tabs, the second state and verifier overwrite the first, and tab 1 gets "This sign-in link has expired".
- The narrow PKCE failure is real too: a second auth that starts after code 1 arrives but before `finishAuth` reads the verifier would fail.
- When it can occur: MCP clients send `initialize` alone and wait for its result. So the first sign-in has one request in flight.
  - The concurrent case needs tokens to vanish mid-session while several tool calls are in flight, for example the refresh-family revocation the session flagged as a "known limit".
  - With a valid refresh token the SDK refreshes rather than redirecting, so no tab opens.
- Never exercised: every e2e run sent one request at a time.
- Deduping at `state()` or `redirectToAuthorization` was not discussed.

unresolved.question: `answerWithError` returns early for anything that is not a request, and nothing logs it, so a failed notification (e.g. `notifications/initialized` or a cancellation) vanishes without a stderr line. Deliberate, or an oversight?
unresolved.note:
The transcript does not cover it: no discussion of notification failures or logging. What follows is inference from code.

The premise is only partly true. SDK 1.32.2 `StreamableHTTPClientTransport.send()` wraps everything in `catch (error) { this.onerror?.(error); throw error; }` (streamableHttp.js lines 427-429). The bridge's `remote.onerror` prints `Seerly MCP: <message>` for anything that is not an `UnauthorizedError`. So a notification whose POST fails gets a stderr line from that path, even though `answerWithError` returns early.

What does go unlogged for a notification is a failure inside `Bridge.signIn()`:
- Consent denied or an `error=` callback: `nextCode()` rejects.
- `finishAuth()` failing on token exchange or PKCE. finishAuth throws without calling onerror.

For a request those reach the app as a JSON-RPC error; for a notification they vanish.

The early return itself matches JSON-RPC, since a notification cannot be answered. The bridge doc's rationale ("so the app never waits on it") only concerns requests. Whether the missing log on that path was deliberate is not stated.

unresolved.question: CredentialStore keys the file by sha256 of the full server URL, project included, so each pinned project (`npx @seerly/mcp acme.com`) registers its own OAuth client and needs its own browser sign-in, against a backend cap of 20 registrations per window. Was per-URL (rather than per-origin) keying a decision in the session, or a side effect?
unresolved.note:
Not a discussed decision. The conversation never mentions per-URL vs per-origin keying. The only statement is the doc comment the session wrote in credential-store.ts: "The registered OAuth client and the tokens for one server URL". Pinned mode was never run: every e2e run passed no project argument. So the separate registration and sign-in per pinned project was never observed.

Relevant facts the session did read:
- The backend caps dynamic registrations at `MAX_REGISTRATIONS_PER_WINDOW = 20` with a 1-hour `REGISTRATION_WINDOW_SECONDS` (origin/main oauth-client.service.ts).
- An unused client is forgotten after 90 days.
- The SDK sends a `resource` parameter. The unpinned authorize URL carried `resource=https://seerly.app/api/mcp`, and prod protected-resource metadata advertises `resource: https://seerly.app/api/mcp`.

Inference:
- Per-URL keying is the simplest correct choice if the tokens are bound to the URL's resource.
- Whether a pinned URL's metadata reports a different resource, and whether the backend checks it, was not verified. A grep of a local airo-backend checkout found `resource` stored on the grant, but no audience check. That checkout is not main.
- So per-origin sharing may well be possible, but it is unverified.

Why it is per-URL is open: a decision or a side effect is not stated.

unresolved.question: npm/README.md says credentials are "readable only by you", which rests on mode 0600/0700 in CredentialStore; Node ignores those modes on Windows, so the file inherits the profile ACL there. Was Windows in scope for 0.1.0, and was that README claim checked against it?
unresolved.note:
Windows was never discussed in the conversation, and the README claim was not checked against it. I grepped the session for Windows, win32 and ACL: the only hit is the code the session wrote. `open-browser.ts` has a `win32` branch using `rundll32 url.dll,FileProtocolHandler`, so Windows was nominally targeted. Nothing ran on Windows; all runs were macOS.

The "readable only by you" line was verified on macOS only. The e2e listing showed the credential file as `-rw-------` inside a `drwx------` `~/.seerly/mcp`.

Inference about Windows:
- Node's `mode` on Windows only maps the write bit to read-only, so 0600 and 0700 do nothing there.
- The file sits under `%USERPROFILE%\.seerly\mcp` and inherits the profile's ACL. By default that is the user, SYSTEM and Administrators, so the claim is roughly true for a default profile but does not hold strictly.

Whether Windows is in scope for 0.1.0 is not stated; the developer needs to answer that.
